questions.q: Who was Kabir (fo|kifr), and what are the two most defining aspects of his identity that appear in his poetry?
questions.a: Kabir was a 15th‑century poet‑saint from Kashi, born into a weaver (julaha) family, and a central figure of the Nirgun Bhakti tradition. The two defining aspects are his low‑caste artisan background and his radical monotheism that rejected both Hindu idol‑worship and Muslim ritual formalism. A wrong answer (e.g., “Kabir was a Brahmin priest who wrote in Sanskrit”) reveals a fundamental factual gap — the student has not grasped the social location that fuels Kabir’s subversive voice.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what “Sadhukkari” (सधुक्करी) language is and why Kabir chose it for his compositions.
questions.a: Sadhukkari is a mixed, utilitarian dialect that blends Braj, Avadhi, Khari Boli, Persian, and Arabic vocabulary — essentially the spoken lingua franca of medieval North Indian mystics and traders. Kabir used it to bypass elite linguistic gatekeepers (Sanskrit, Persian) and speak directly to common people in their everyday tongue. A wrong answer (e.g., “Sadhukkari is just another name for Braj Bhasha”) shows the student misses the deliberate inclusivity and anti‑hierarchical intent behind Kabir’s language choice.

questions.q: The first poem in the chapter opens with the line “eksjk fivre iklA” (इस जक फिवरे इकल). Using your knowledge of Kabir’s context, identify the metaphor implied by “fivre” (फिवरे) and explain what it suggests about the human condition.
questions.a: “Fivre” (फिवरे) means a weaver’s loom or the act of weaving. Given Kabir’s julaha background, the metaphor casts human life as a fabric being woven on the loom of time — each breath a shuttle throw, each action a thread. The poem urges the reader to “see” (इकल) this process before the cloth is finished (death). A student who answers “fivre means a market” or “it refers to a temple” fails to transfer biographical knowledge to textual interpretation — a classic application error.

questions.q: Compare the social critique implicit in Kabir’s use of “lkvksu ekl” (लकवसु एकल) — the weaver’s courtyard — with the courtly settings of classical Sanskrit kavya. What does this shift of setting reveal about the intended audience and poetic purpose?
questions.a: Classical kavya typically unfolds in royal courts, gardens, or temples, addressing patrons and connoisseurs. Kabir’s “lkvksu ekl” (the weaver’s modest workspace) grounds the poem in labor and domesticity, signalling that his audience is the ordinary artisan, not the elite. This shift reveals a democratic poetic purpose: to awaken spiritual insight amid daily work, not to entertain aristocrats. A student who only notes “different setting” without linking it to audience and purpose has not analysed the sociological dimension.

questions.q: Critique the view that Kabir’s poetry is “simple” because it uses common words. Use evidence from the vocabulary list (e.g., “fifjr”, “c[kkfuv”, “fugkjy”) to argue whether simplicity of vocabulary equals simplicity of thought.
questions.a: The vocabulary list shows words like “fifjr” (इज़हर/अभिव्यक्ति), “c[kkfuv” (चककुफ़/चखना), “fugkjy” (फुगक्य/देखना) — these are everyday verbs, but they are deployed in dense metaphysical arguments (e.g., “tue vcfèk ge :i fugkjy u;u u frjfir Hksy” — “You have not seen the true form, so you are not satisfied”). The thought is complex: the epistemology of direct perception versus hearsay, the futility of ritual. Equating simple diction with simple thought is a category error. A student who agrees with the “simple poetry” view misses the philosophical depth encoded in accessible language.

questions.q: Write a four‑line stanza in Sadhukkari‑style Hindi (mixing Braj, Khari Boli, and one Persian/Arabic word) that uses a weaver’s metaphor to convey the idea “time does not wait for anyone.” Do not copy Kabir; create your own image.
questions.a:
Example:
“निस दिन ताना बाना रे, काल करे नहिं देर।
साँझ भई चरखा छूटा, कह कबीर सुन ले शेर॥”
(Uses Braj “निस दिन”, Khari Boli “काल करे नहिं देर”, Persian “शेर” for lion/courage, and the weaver’s “ताना बाना”.) A poor answer would be a direct lift from Kabir or a stanza without any mixed vocabulary, showing the student cannot synthesise the linguistic concept creatively.
